selected.RECENTLY_USED_CHECK: Ma l9inach had topic f memory files li t9raw.
KEY_EVIDENCE: 79 randomized controlled trials, N=1,356,521, across climate mitigation, health, performance and service behaviours.
Short term versus passive controls: Hedges g=0.17, 95% CI 0.11-0.23, k=37.
Short term versus active controls: g=0.23, 95% CI 0.15-0.31, k=42.
Active-control synthesis had I2=96% and small-study-effect concern; trim-and-fill estimate stayed positive at g=0.15.
GRADE certainty ranged from low to moderate.
CONTRADICTORY_EVIDENCE: High unexplained heterogeneity limits blanket claims.
Some trials had risk-of-bias issues and most data came from high-income countries.
selected.UNCERTAINTY: Mechanisms, individual response, transfer to Morocco and long-term durability are not fully established.
selected.CONTEXT: Social comparison interventions show people how their behaviour compares with others, for example energy use, health behaviour or performance.
selected.CONFIDENCE: high for a small average effect; medium for transfer to a specific setting
selected.EXACT_TITLE: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examining social comparison as a behaviour change technique across the behavioural sciences
selected.AUTHORS: Thole H. Hoppen, Rieke M. Cuno, Janna Nelson, Frederike Lemmel, Pascal Schlechter, Nexhmedin Morina et al.
selected.RESEARCH_QUESTION: Ch7al social-comparison behaviour-change techniques kaybdlo actual behaviour?
selected.STUDY_TYPE: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
selected.METHOD: MEDLINE, PsycINFO and Web of Science search to January 2024; PRISMA selection; Hedges g; risk-of-bias, GRADE, moderator analyses, Egger test and trim-and-fill.
selected.MAIN_RESULT: Average behaviour change was small but statistically significant versus passive and active controls.
selected.EFFECT_SIZE: g=0.17 versus passive controls; g=0.23 versus active controls; active-control trim-and-fill g=0.15.
selected.LIMITATIONS: High heterogeneity, some risk-of-bias, possible publication bias in active-control synthesis and limited geographic generalizability.
selected.CRITICISM: Pooled group effects do not mean every individual changes behaviour.
selected.REPLICATION_STATUS: Synthesis of multiple independent RCTs rather than a single-study replication.
selected.CORRELATION_VS_CAUSATION: RCT evidence supports causal intervention effects at trial level, with heterogeneity limiting universal claims.
selected.GENERALIZABILITY: Medium-low outside studied high-income settings until local replication.
selected.WHAT_WE_CAN_CONCLUDE: Social-comparison interventions can produce a small average behaviour change in the intended direction.
selected.WHAT_WE_CANNOT_CONCLUDE: The effect is not proven large, universal or identical across cultures and behaviours.
selected.WHY_IT_MATTERS: Low-cost nudges can help, but design, context and realistic expectations matter.

SOURCE_ORIGINS: Mission archeologique maroco-francaise / Ministere de la Culture francais
Annals of the Association of American Geographers / Lightfoot and Miller
KEY_EVIDENCE: Sijilmasa was in Tafilalt near Rissani with long occupation from roughly the 8th to 15th centuries.
Medieval texts and archaeology link its early polity to Miknasa and Banu Midrar with a Sufri emirate.
It became a major caravan entrepot connecting Sahel and Maghreb and was strongly tied to the gold trade.
Almoravid conquest in the mid-11th century increased its strategic role; minting was important.
Lightfoot and Miller link rise and fall not only to trade but also water, agriculture, oasis ecology and social organization.
CONTRADICTORY_EVIDENCE: Exact foundation and destruction dates vary by textual tradition.
A single-cause Atlantic-trade explanation for decline is too simple.
Archaeology can constrain narratives built only from chronicles.
selected.UNCERTAINTY: Exact population, annual trade volume, early chronology and one single cause of decline are not securely quantified.
selected.CONTEXT: Sijilmasa was an oasis polity, market, mint and strategic node linking Morocco, the Sahara, West Africa and the Mediterranean.
selected.CONFIDENCE: high on broad role and chronology; medium on precise early dates and scale
selected.FEATURE_OPENING_MATERIAL: Bla port w bla b7ar, Sijilmasa kanat katkhddm b7al port f wast l-yabsa: caravans kaywslou men Sahara b-dahab w goods, w kaykhrjo men Tafilalt l-north.
SECTION_OUTLINE: Tafilalt qbl Sijilmasa: oasis, water and routes
Miknasa, Banu Midrar and Sufri emirate
Why Sijilmasa matters for Morocco-Africa history
KEY_FACTS: Traditional foundation window in the mid-8th century.
Strong connection to gold trade and minting.
Almoravid conquest in the mid-11th century.
TIMELINE: 8th-10th c.: Midrarid/Sufri polity and caravan growth.
INTERPRETATIONS: Trade-first: growth came from a key trans-Saharan terminus.
Oasis-infrastructure: trade depended on water, agriculture and local organization.
State-power: control mattered because gold, minting and caravan taxation supported rulers.
COUNTERINTERPRETATIONS: Saharan routes were not fixed; security, ecology and politics shifted them.
Sijilmasa is not only a Moroccan story; it is also West African and Mediterranean history.
MYTH_VS_EVIDENCE: DOCUMENTED FACT: major caravan hub and oasis city.
LIKELY INTERPRETATION: gold flows strengthened rulers who controlled it.
CONTESTED INTERPRETATION: exact moment and single cause of decline.
MEMORY/LEGEND: neat founding stories need source labels.
UNKNOWN: reliable population counts and annual trade volumes.
selected.PRESENT_DAY_RELEVANCE: Kaybayan belli Morocco-Africa relations 3andhom roots twila f movement, commerce and shared systems across Sahara.

selected.PROPOSED_TITLE: Tayeb Saddiki w l-halqa: kifach masra7 Maghribi 7awl ykoun modern bla ma y9ta3 m3a l-forma cha3biya
selected.WHY_SELECTED: Substantial postcolonial theatre topic: translation, halqa, oral performance, zajal, diglossia, Moliere, Moroccan plurality, audience relation and criticism.
selected.RECENTLY_USED_CHECK: literature-used fih Rabat World Book Capital 2026 w Gnawa b mode preproduction; Tayeb Saddiki ma kaynach.
SOURCE_ORIGINS: Lamalif interview anthology / Liverpool University Press
KEY_EVIDENCE: Saddiki discussed Moroccan theatre as a field searching for its own form and audience after colonial and anticolonial performance histories.
Recent IMIST analysis treats halqa as a dramaturgical principle: circularity, orality, improvisation, audience interaction, fragmented narration, polyphony and diglossia.
Scholarship connects Diwan Sidi Abderrahman al-Majdoub to transposition of halqa aesthetics into institutional theatre.
Work on Saddiki and Moliere shows appropriation and transformation rather than simple imitation.
Jean-Francois Clement provides a counterpoint: precolonial spectacles such as halqa and bsat should not automatically be called theatre in the same modern institutional sense.
CONTRADICTORY_EVIDENCE: The idea of an uninterrupted authentic Moroccan theatre genealogy is contested.
Saddiki did not simply reject Europe; he also used Moliere, adaptation and Western stage conventions.
Institutional funding, television and audience change also matter for theatre history.
selected.UNCERTAINTY: Reception varies by play, decade and audience, so blanket claims about all Moroccan audiences should be avoided.
selected.CONTEXT: Post-independence Moroccan theatre had to negotiate imported stage forms and local performance repertoires. Saddiki sits inside that tension rather than on only one side.
selected.CONFIDENCE: high on documented aesthetic synthesis; medium on broad national-reception claims
selected.FEATURE_OPENING_MATERIAL: Mlli l-jomhour kaywlli da2ira 7awl l-performance, l-7d bin stage w street kaytbddl. Saddiki khda l-halqa b7al principle dyal writing and performance, machi ghir decoration.
SECTION_OUTLINE: What halqa is and is not
Moliere as dialogue rather than copy
Later influence and why it matters now
selected.CONTEXT_DETAIL: Popular performance forms existed before modern theatre institutions; the feature must distinguish those two histories.
selected.CREATOR_OR_WORK_BACKGROUND: Tayeb Saddiki (1939-2016) was a Moroccan playwright, director, actor and adaptor.
CENTRAL_IDEAS: Cultural identity can be built through appropriation and transformation rather than isolation.
Orality and audience interaction are formal devices, not only heritage decoration.
Moroccan cultural plurality appears in language, repertoire and performance traditions.
selected.HISTORICAL_RELATIONSHIP: His theatre can be read against colonial transplantation of European stage forms and post-independence search for cultural autonomy.
selected.RECEPTION: Scholarship treats Saddiki as a major Moroccan and Arab theatre figure, but reception claims should stay specific to works and institutions.
selected.CRITICISM: Clement warns against retroactively calling every old spectacle theatre; this prevents nationalist myth-making.
COMPETING_INTERPRETATIONS: Saddiki as recuperator of indigenous theatrical roots.
Saddiki as hybrid modernist combining local and imported repertoires.
Critical view: uninterrupted native-theatre genealogy can be conceptually misleading.
selected.LATER_INFLUENCE: Halqa, festive forms and heritage adaptation remain reference points in Moroccan and Maghrebi theatre debates.
selected.WHY_IT_MATTERS_TODAY: The same question remains: kifach creator yst3ml heritage bla folklore freeze, w kifach ykoun global bla cultural copy.
CLAIMS_TO_AVOID: Halqa is identical to modern theatre.
All Moroccan theatre follows his model.
